notes.meaning: The prophet sees a glorious warrior approaching from Edom and its chief city, Bozrah. His robes are stained bright red, and He marches forward in tremendous strength. He announces that He is the Lord, who speaks the truth and has full power to rescue His people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical scholars view verses 1–6 as a separate poem that was placed here independently of the surrounding text.

notes.meaning: The prophet asks why this royal conqueror is wearing clothes stained deep red like a worker stomping grapes in a winepress. In Bible times, people stomped grapes with their feet to squeeze out juice, splashing red liquid all over their garments. Here, the red stains show that a serious act of judgment has just occurred.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some early church fathers and Catholic writings view the trampled red garments as a picture of Christ suffering in His Passion, where His own blood was poured out for our salvation.

notes.meaning: The Lord answers that He crushed the hostile nations just like a man stomping grapes in a pit all by himself. No human ally stepped forward to help Him carry out this judgment. The red splashes on His garments are the blood of His enemies, whom He brought down in His holy anger.

The Lord explains that He had set a fixed time to punish oppressors and rescue His people. He executed judgment on evil so that those He bought back could finally be set free. His vengeance lasts only a day, but the rescue and blessing He brings lasts like a full year.

The Lord looked across the world and found no human helper willing or able to defend what is right. He was appalled that no one stood up to support the needy. Because human help failed completely, His own mighty arm and righteous anger brought full deliverance.

The Lord trampled the rebellious nations in His anger and poured out their lifeblood onto the earth. He made them stagger as if they were made drunk by drinking the cup of His wrath. This image shows that no earthly kingdom can stand against God when He decides to judge wickedness.

The speaker pauses to lead the community in a heartfelt prayer of praise. He remembers the Lord's faithful, covenant love and all the wonderful deeds He performed for Israel throughout history. When believers face hard times, they can find strength by recalling God's past mercy.

The Lord chose Israel to be His own special family, expecting them to be loyal children who would not deceive Him. Because of this covenant promise, He stepped forward and acted as their Savior. He treated them with fatherly trust, hoping they would honor their relationship with Him.

Whenever His people went through pain, the Lord shared their distress and felt deep sympathy for them. He sent the Angel of His Presence to rescue them and carried them like a loving father through all the days of old. This shows how deeply God cares for His people when they suffer.

In spite of God's kindness, the people rebelled against Him and caused deep grief to His Holy Spirit. Because of their stubborn disobedience, God turned against them and fought them as an enemy. When people persist in sin, God must discipline them to bring them back to their senses.

In their time of suffering, the people remembered the ancient days when Moses led the nation. They asked where the Lord was who had guided their ancestors safely through the Red Sea. They longed to see the power of the One who placed His Holy Spirit among their leaders.

The people recalled how God sent His glorious power to guide Moses and part the sea before them. Walking through the divided waters delivered Israel and displayed God's greatness to all nations. God performed this wonder to make an everlasting name for Himself.

God guided the people straight through the deep bed of the sea without any stumbling. The dry path across the seabed was as smooth and safe for them as an open, flat plain is for a running horse. His guiding hand kept them from tripping over any obstacle.

The Spirit of the Lord brought the weary people safely into the Promised Land, giving them quiet rest like cattle resting in a green valley. God led them gently through every hardship until their travels were finished. He did all this to display His glory and prove His faithfulness.

The prophet begs God to look down from His holy and glorious throne in heaven. He asks why God's passionate love and mighty strength seem hidden, and why His mercy feels held back. This is an honest prayer asking God not to stay distant while His people are hurting.

The prayer confesses that the Lord is the true Father and Redeemer of His people. Even if their earthly ancestors like Abraham or Jacob could not know them or help them now, God remains their eternal Father. His very name and character have always meant rescue for His children.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: George Leo Haydock explained that Abraham would not acknowledge ungodly descendants as his true children, nor does he possess the divine power to rescue them.

notes.meaning: The people cry out and ask why the Lord has permitted them to stray from His ways and let their hearts grow hard. They know they have no power to return on their own, so they plead with God to come back to them. They ask for mercy for the sake of the covenant family He chose as His inheritance.

differ.view: Methodists teach that God does not cause people to sin, but allows them to wander and harden by withdrawing His restraining grace when they stubbornly reject Him.
Reformed Christians teach that this hardening is God's active judicial punishment, whereby He hands rebellious sinners over to their own desires and Satan as a judgment for sin.

notes.meaning: The people mourn that they possessed the holy land and temple for only a short time compared to God's eternal promises. Now, brutal enemy armies have marched in and trampled God's holy sanctuary. They plead with God to step in because His sacred house has been ruined.

The prayer ends with the painful cry that Israel has become like a foreign nation that God never ruled. It feels as though they were never called by His name or known as His own family. They express this deep grief to urge God to return and rule over them once again.
